                    ### Question
                    A 3-day-old newborn is brought to the physician because of abdominal distention, inconsolable crying, and 3 episodes of bilious vomiting since the previous evening. He was delivered at home at 40 weeks' gestation by a trained midwife. He has not passed meconium. Physical examination shows abdominal distention, a tight anal sphincter, and an explosive passage of air and feces on removal of the examining finger. Abnormal development of which of the following best explains this patient's condition?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Muscularis mucosae and serosa
opb. Epithelium and lamina propria
opc. Submucosa and muscularis externa
opd. Epithelium and submucosa
ope. Muscularis mucosae and lamina propria

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's presentation with abdominal distention, bilious vomiting, inconsolable crying, absence of meconium passage, tight anal sphincter, and explosive passage of air and feces on rectal examination is highly suggestive of Hirschsprung disease. This condition involves the absence of ganglion cells in the submucosa and muscularis externa of the colon, leading to functional obstruction. The abnormal development of submucosa and muscularis externa best explains the patient's symptoms.
